channel.title: EverythingTech
channel.description: A daily tech newspaper. 45+ sources, read in full and edited by an LLM every morning.

item.title: Binance's postmortem: fake job interviews and an internal AI tool let hackers take $6.3 billion
item.description:
The breach began in June with a tampered installer, but the theft only succeeded in October after attackers turned Binance's own internal AI tool against its wallets.

Our earlier coverage of this heist reported the suspended withdrawals and the FBI's attribution to North Korea, but not how the attackers got in. Binance's postmortem now sets out the chain. In June, a developer downloaded an installer that appears to have been served through a malicious search ad. Binance says its security team caught that first infection and replaced the machine. What its tools missed was a zero-day payload that swapped a Python environment executable for a malicious version, giving the attackers a backdoor the endpoint protection did not flag.

The second route was social. In September, someone posing as a recruiter ran a months-long hiring process with another engineer, including calls, several rounds of interviews and shared social media pages to build trust, before sending a take-home assignment that was malware. The FBI links the campaign to a North Korean unit it calls TraderTraitor. By October 20, the attackers were using Binance's internal AI tool to take control of wallets belonging to the first compromised engineer and a third employee, and on October 29 they logged into that third employee's computer to launch the transfer.

The reported loss makes this the largest crypto theft on record, but the method is the lesson. It ran through a developer laptop, a development tool and an internal tool that held wallet control. The postmortem does not explain how that AI tool came to have the authority it used, and that is the question other exchanges will need to answer for their own systems.

item.title: Claude's message threads cut first-token delay about 35% on long sessions, and token bills stay the same
item.description:
The feature changes what gets sent on each turn, not what gets billed, so the gain is latency for long agent sessions.

Anthropic has put message threads into public beta on the Claude Platform. Until now, an agent making hundreds of requests in one session resent its entire history every time. With a thread, the client sends the conversation once, then each later request carries only the new messages and the ID of the previous response. The server holds the thread in memory, encrypted and never written to disk, and it expires five minutes after its last request. If a thread expires, the client has to resend the full conversation to start a new one.

The gain grows with context size. Anthropic says that for most Claude Code users, where threads are on by default, requests between 500,000 and one million tokens saw median time to first token fall by about 35 percent. Anthropic is explicit that the model still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage does not change. ZDNet and The New Stack covered the same launch with headlines that ask whether the speed-up holds for real Claude Code logs and whether the bill changes. Anthropic's own description answers the second question: it does not.

The five-minute expiry sets the limit on the feature. A session that pauses longer than that pays for a full resend, so the benefit is concentrated in active work. Anthropic names three cases: long coding agents, computer-use agents that keep screenshots in the thread, and document-heavy workflows.

item.title: Maple moved 287,000 lines of React to Foldkit in three days, and the comparison harness was the real job
item.description:
Claude wrote the new app in three days, but most of Maple's own effort went into a harness that decided when each screen matched the old one.

Maple left React in October. Its web app was roughly 287,000 lines spread over 131 routes, and Claude handled the rewrite in just three days. The team says the writing was the quick part; the heavier lifting went into a comparison tool that checked old against new, pixel for pixel and for behavior and accessibility, and decided when each screen counted as finished. That harness compared more than 2,600 screen variants.

The trigger was a crash. In August, the errors page went down in production with React error #301. The cause was a wrapper object created fresh on every render, which a hook compared by identity while updating state mid-render, so the two kept re-triggering each other. The fix took a day, yet nothing prevented the next instance. The codebase carried roughly 520 hook calls across 208 files, so tracing what an org switch does to an in-flight query meant reading each component in render order.

Foldkit is The Elm Architecture on top of Effect, which the rest of Maple already used. All state sits in one Model, and one update function is the only code allowed to change it. Events arrive as past-tense messages such as ClickedRow or SucceededLoadLogs. Commands are the only code that talks to the network, and their results come back as more messages. The team argues that this matters more now that agents write much of the frontend and make the same hook mistakes people do.

item.title: Postman's desktop app reportedly installed AI plugins into coding agents and tried to share API data
item.description:
A routine desktop app is said to have added plugins to Claude Code and OpenAI Codex without asking, which turns Postman into a question about agent permissions.

A developer opened Postman and then found that two AI coding agents, Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, had changed without their permission, with Postman's desktop app having installed plugins into both. A Hacker News thread about the same episode drew more than a thousand points, and its headline says the app also attempts to share all API data. The details here come from the headline and standfirst only, because the full articles could not be read. The scope of the data-sharing claim is therefore unverified.

The concern is specific. Postman collections often hold API keys, bearer tokens and internal endpoint URLs. A coding agent running with the developer's permissions can read those, so a plugin installed without consent gives an agent a new path to them.

item.title: Cloudflare halved DNS change propagation and cut builder memory 85% with a planner that rebuilds only what it can prove
item.description:
Zone-wide rebuilds for setting-only changes are gone, so zones with tens of millions of records no longer stall the pipeline.

Cloudflare's Zone Builder turns each DNS change into data its edge DNS servers can use. The workload has grown. In 2022 the builder received about 250 record changes per second. It now gets about 700, plus about 100 other events such as zone setting changes. The bigger problem was the work some events triggered. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and Cloudflare expects them to reach hundreds of millions, so rebuilding a whole zone on each setting change had become too expensive.

The hard part was proving when a smaller build is safe. A record event names what changed. A zone event is murkier: it may originate in any of several Cloudflare products, it may not explain itself, and it can touch data that several same-named zones share. Over-scoping wastes capacity, while under-scoping risks stale records at the edge. Cloudflare built a planner that picks the smallest build it can prove safe, plus a scheduler that merges work for the same zone.

Together the changes cut peak memory by 85%. That headroom made it safe to cut back on delays the pipeline had long built in as protection, and the time from a DNS change to data landing in Quicksilver was halved. Back in 2022, per-record builds had already run 150 times faster than full builds on average.

item.title: BlackX bootkit beat Secure Boot on fully patched Windows machines, exposing a revocation gap
item.description:
The malware runs before Windows loads, on machines that had every Microsoft patch for the flaw it uses, which makes the revocation step the real question.

BlackX is a UEFI bootkit that infected Windows machines with all known patches installed. It exploits Baton Drop, a logic flaw in the Windows boot manager tracked as CVE-2022-21894, which lets attackers bypass Secure Boot and in some conditions extract BitLocker keys. Microsoft fixed that flaw in 2022, but it did not revoke trust in the certificate that signed older vulnerable boot managers. BlackLotus used that gap in 2023 to load a malicious kernel-mode driver. Microsoft then issued more updates in 2023 and 2024, adding a new certificate and a way to revoke trust in the old one.

The BlackX victims had installed those updates, which is the puzzle. Ars Technica frames the question as whether Microsoft's unclear guidance about Secure Boot protections is to blame, rather than the individual machines.

item.title: Goldman Sachs restricts Claude Code for bankers and traders, with quant strats exempt
item.description:
Replit's CEO says finance is moving to ban coding agents on employee machines, but he cites no incident behind Goldman's decision.

Bloomberg reported that Goldman Sachs has restricted engineers' access to Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub coding tools. The restriction covers bankers and traders, while certain quantitative employees known as strats are exempt. A Goldman spokesperson told Bloomberg the bank weighs productivity gains against risk when it decides which employees can keep using AI tools.

Replit CEO Amjad Masad said on X that agents running on employee endpoints are becoming a systemic security risk, and that finance is moving toward bans, with supply-chain attacks as the driver. He offered no example of an incident that prompted Goldman's decision, so the reason is unconfirmed. The underlying concern is clear: a coding agent on a laptop can read the credentials stored there and run dependencies nobody reviewed. Vercel has set a deadline for its suppliers to drop long-lived keys for the same reason.

item.title: Anthropic confirms a Claude Code prompt change against recreating games, and developers report wider refusals
item.description:
Developers say Opus 5.5 now refuses reverse-engineering work it used to handle, and Anthropic has not said whether those refusals share the same cause.

Addy Osmani, who works on Anthropic's technical team, confirmed on X that the company added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt for Opus 5.5. They steer the model away from recreating someone else's specific game, which Anthropic treats as infringement under its usage policy. He said developers can still make original games, work in established genres, and use their own designs and assets.

The complaints go further. One developer says paid client projects stalled because Claude Code will not work on existing games. Another says Opus 5.5 refuses software-analysis tasks that worked before. One developer returned to work by switching to Opus 4.8. Anthropic has not said whether the reverse-engineering refusals come from the new instructions or from separate cybersecurity restrictions.

The change is narrow on paper, and the open question is how far it reaches. Developers working on legacy code or interoperability are the most likely to hit it first. Osmani invited developers to contact him when Claude refuses work on their own creations.

item.title: Fal doubles its valuation to $16 billion on a $1.3 billion round as inference demand climbs
item.description:
Fal's valuation doubled in four months, but the sector's thin gross margins are the number that decides whether the price holds.

Fal, a San Francisco startup that hosts and runs AI video, image and audio models, raised $1.3 billion in a round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with Nvidia, Sound Ventures and T. Rowe Price also participating. The round was announced alongside a Series E, bringing the total raised across both to $1.65 billion. The valuation is $16 billion, double the $8 billion it reached in April, according to Bloomberg.

Demand for inference, which means running an already trained model to produce output, is the driver, particularly from customers using open-weight models. Bloomberg reported that Fal passed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year. Rivals Baseten, Fireworks AI and Modal are also raising at higher valuations, but their gross margins remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease, according to people familiar with their finances.

A valuation at this level assumes Fal can turn demand into margin. The thin margins across the category are the figure to watch.

item.title: Canva is cutting or relocating 1,271 people, 22 percent of staff, to refound the company around small teams
item.description:
Canva is merging its product, growth and platform teams and pushing hybrid staff toward two or three office days a week from January.

Co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins announced that Canva is making changes that affect 1,271 people, which is 22 percent of its staff. Some people will have different roles or be asked to relocate to centralised hubs, and others will be laid off. Leavers get at least six months of salary and twelve months of healthcare cover, plus career support.

Perkins framed the move as a refounding, saying small changes were not enough. Product, Growth and Platform teams are merging into one product organization, layers are being removed, and Sydney becomes the primary home for more product teams. Starting in January, Canva expects most hybrid employees to spend two to three days a week in an office.

Squarespace announced layoffs covering 19 percent of its staff the day before. The reporting ties Canva's cuts to reorganization rather than to AI, so the cause is restructuring as stated by the company.

item.title: SUSE plans to cut about 10% of its 1,900 staff, citing automation and AI
item.description:
The open source vendor says automation and AI are reducing the need for some roles, and it is flattening management to cut overhead.

SUSE plans to cut roughly 10 percent of its 1,900-person global workforce. CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen wrote that automation and AI are reducing the need for some roles, and that the company will run with less overhead and flatter management. He called the decisions painful for staff and for the open source community. The details here come from the headline and standfirst, because the full article could not be read, so which roles are affected is not covered.

Squarespace announced layoffs the same week, but explicit ties to AI are less consistent in its case.

item.title: Vitest 5 cuts test times 8 to 25 percent but flips defaults that break existing suites
item.description:
The speed gains come from a shared Vite server and reused VM code, while the breaking defaults mostly expose tests that were already wrong.

VoidZero's Vitest 5.0 is mostly about speed. Benchmarks across projects from a five-file package to a 1,280-module monolith show roughly 8 to 25 percent faster runs, and up to 53 percent in VM pools. Much of that comes from inline projects sharing one Vite server, a now-stable disk cache for modules, and VM pools that reuse compiled code instead of recompiling. A new vitest doctor command reruns a suite under other configurations and suggests the quicker ones.

Several defaults tightened as well. clearMocks is now on by default, a promise assertion that is never awaited errors out instead of warning, vi.mock calls hoisted out of the top level throw, and an empty string passed to toThrow matches any error. The toolchain floor moved too: Vite 6.4 and Node.js 22.12 at minimum, and Yarn users must install vite themselves. Reporter output and blob reports now sit under one .vitest/ directory, so CI jobs that read artifact paths need the new location.

The risky cases are suites that pass on Vitest 4 and then fail in CI with errors that say nothing about why. Call-count assertions that relied on mock history leaking between tests are the usual casualty. Ecosystem packages lag too: Cloudflare's vitest-pool-workers pins its peer range to v4, so projects using it fail before any test runs.

item.title: ChatGPT will merge its Chat and Work tabs and pool usage with Codex
item.description:
Codex stays a separate app, but both products will draw from one token allowance, so heavy users may wait for resets more often.

OpenAI emailed users that it is preparing to merge the Chat and Work tabs inside the ChatGPT desktop app. The change will reach select users first for feedback. OpenAI's stated goal is to let people move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, with files, plugins and web tasks in one place. Codex remains a separate experience within the desktop app.

The usage change matters more to heavy users. ChatGPT and Codex will draw tokens from the same allowance pool. OpenAI says most users will not notice, but depending on usage and model, some people may need to wait for resets more often. Anthropic merged Claude's chat and Cowork screens in September, so OpenAI is following the same path.

item.title: A single exec tool is replacing agent tool catalogs, letting models chain actions in one script
item.description:
Instead of one tool call per turn, the model writes a short script that chains dependent actions inside a sandbox.

For two years, building an agent meant designing many tools and tuning each schema. The author argues that is ending: agents now squeeze their whole catalog into a single exec(code) tool, a pattern called Code Mode or programmatic tool calling. Instead of firing tools one at a time across turns, the model drafts a brief TypeScript or Python program that links actions together, waits on each step, and runs it inside a contained sandbox.

The gain is in turns. Standard tool calling takes one action per turn, and each result goes back into the prompt before the next decision. The article's examples show a research task that queries sources, filters irrelevant hits and extracts the answer in one script, and a multi-file edit that applies coordinated changes, runs a check, and branches on pass or fail in a single pass.

The trade-off sits in the sandbox. One exec tool means model-written code runs with whatever the sandbox can reach, so the sandbox's network and credential access decides how safe the pattern is. The article makes the efficiency case, and the security side is the part to check.

item.title: Google will switch AI off by default in K-12 products, but blocking AI also removes Search
item.description:
Schools that want Search will have to accept Gemini as well, because Google bundles the AI features and the search box under one switch.

K-12 schools on Google's education products will start with AI switched off. Administrators will have to turn the features on by hand, a change that lands in the coming months. The switch covers Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search, and administrators cannot choose among them.

That bundling is the catch. A school cannot keep Search while turning off the chatbots, so any school that blocks AI entirely gives up Search too. Google presents the change as a response to educators, researchers and lawmakers. The same logic runs through Google's consumer product, where an AI Overview appears at the top of most results and AI Mode is pushed as the direction of Search.

item.title: Nexus Mods will require AI disclosure on new mod uploads but stops short of a ban
item.description:
AI-assisted mods must now carry a public explanation of how and where AI was used, and the AI tags get more prominent on mod pages.

Nexus Mods will require authors of newly uploaded mods to declare whether AI was used in their work. Mods tagged AI-assisted must also include a public explanation of how and where AI was used, and the tags will appear more prominently on mod pages. Owner Victor Folmann says the site is pro-human creativity but will not ban AI-generated mods.

Folmann's reasoning is that AI now touches scripting, textures, voices and full assets, so the line between acceptable and unacceptable is hard to draw. A ban would not remove AI from modding, he argues, only stop people from saying so. Nexus says it will not use mods to train AI or license them to anyone who does, and it is working on clearer control over how other authors reuse mods. It is also limiting how many mods from one author appear in Recently Added and tightening uploads from new accounts, because mod production is speeding up.

item.title: Data centers are burning rebuilt jet engines for power as grid waits stretch to seven years
item.description:
A converted jet turbine can have a data center running in about 24 months, while a 100-megawatt grid hookup in Northern Virginia takes about seven years.

Waiting years for grid hookups and new turbines, some AI data centers now generate their own power from converted jet engines, according to the New York Times. The engines are retired aircraft units rebuilt to burn natural gas. They are not permanent plants, but they are fast. A Rystad Energy analyst said a jet-powered unit can have a data center running in 24 months. Hooking 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia takes about seven years, according to the International Energy Agency.

The delays already cost projects. Microsoft pulled out as anchor customer for Nscale's data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it could not deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s. xAI has installed eight converted turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center, according to state permits and satellite imagery the Times cited. Crusoe, which is building OpenAI's first Stargate site in Abilene, ordered 13 converted units in April.

The trade-off is efficiency and emissions. TechCrunch describes the approach as less efficient and less environmentally friendly than the alternatives, and the Trump administration is encouraging data centers to generate their own power.

item.title: A 2014 Renault's head unit hid its clock menu, so the owner dug into the firmware
item.description:
The clock option was missing from every menu, and a second settings button only showed a "No maps detected" pop-up.

The author drives a 2014 Renault and started with a clock problem. After daylight saving moved the time out by an hour, the head unit's menus had no Set time option at all. One settings button worked only for Bluetooth and phonebook settings. The second did nothing except show a "No maps detected" pop-up. The previous owner had said the clock needs the navigation SD card, which the author had discarded, and the author did not believe it.

After an hour of searching menus, the author fetched the firmware and started reverse engineering it. The excerpt that could be read ends before the author reports whether the firmware reveals the setting, so the outcome is not covered here.

item.title: CheerpJ 5.0 runs Java 21 and 25 in the browser with a full JDK and an experimental WasmGC engine
item.description:
The new WasmGC engine is experimental in this release, with production readiness planned for CheerpJ 6.0 in early 2027.

CheerpJ 5.0 brings Java 21 and 25 to the browser, completing a roadmap published in February 2025 to reach parity with the latest Java LTS by the end of 2026. It now ships the full JDK for every version, so Java can be compiled in the browser, not just run. CheerpJ is a full JVM compiled to WebAssembly and works at the bytecode level, so source code is not required, and Kotlin and Scala work too.

The bigger technical change is the new WasmGC execution engine, which is experimental in this release. The team will focus on stabilizing it over the next few months, and it becomes production-ready in CheerpJ 6.0, planned for early 2027. The team expects WasmGC to make large Java applications practical in the browser, including modern versions of Minecraft and IntelliJ IDEA. The part of the release that could be read gives no benchmark numbers for the engine, so that expectation rests on the roadmap until 6.0.

item.title: Google's LiteRT Tensor API builds on-device models in C++ that run on CPU, GPU and NPU
item.description:
Google reports its SAM 2 build ran about 1.5 times faster than Apple's MLX on a MacBook Pro, in one benchmark on one model.

Google introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, a C++ library for building, customizing and optimizing models for on-device use. Developers define computation graphs operation by operation, and the same graph can run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU or NPU without a rewrite for each backend. The API can load weights directly from checkpoints, including Hugging Face safetensors files, and supports zero-copy buffers across pre-processing, inference and post-processing.

Google used a coding agent to write a multi-object segmentation and tracking app, and that app doubled as the benchmark. Running the SAM 2 model on GPUs across a MacBook (Metal), an iPhone (Metal) and an Android phone (OpenCL), Google reports the MacBook build ran about 1.5 times faster than Apple's MLX at fp16 precision. Google also argues that plain C++ graphs suit coding agents, which can build, change, check and time a graph by generating code. The benchmark covers one model on three devices, so it does not show how the API performs on other models or hardware.

item.title: Codex users spot a GPT-6.2 Astra entry in usage logs, hinting at a launch OpenAI has not announced
item.description:
The model ID appears only on October 31 usage bars, with its share ranging from 1.6 percent of one user's week to 37.7 percent of a single day for another.

Codex users noticed a new entry, gpt-6.2-astra, in their usage analytics, next to the GPT-6 Astra model that launched in September. It appears only on the October 31 bar. The model picker still says GPT-6 Astra, which suggests some requests are routed quietly, either as an A/B test or a staged rollout.

The evidence is mixed. One user posted a raw response whose model field read gpt-6.2-astra, which suggests the ID is live on OpenAI's servers. OpenAI itself has said nothing about it, and the model documentation still names only GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Testers have shared outputs they attribute to the model, but the picker does not say which model answered, so attribution is unconfirmed. Context matters here: GPT-6.1 Astra was pulled in late September over worries about deception and scope found in internal testing, and a retrained 6.2 is one possibility, though the article calls that speculation.

item.title: Palantir's U.S. commercial revenue passed government revenue for the first time, but contracts are getting shorter
item.description:
Customers are signing shorter contracts that can expand quickly, which CEO Alex Karp described as a faster but less committed pattern.

Palantir reported third-quarter revenue up 96 percent from a year earlier, to $2.31 billion, beating the $2.18 billion analysts expected, and it raised full-year guidance. The clincher was that U.S. commercial revenue, at $984 million and up 148 percent, passed U.S. government revenue of $953 million for the first time. Growth comes from enterprises that want AI software to run frontier models and custom-train open-weight models without sending their data to outside AI labs, plus forward-deployed engineers who customize the product with customers.

The warning sign is contract length. Karp told analysts that customers move faster to deployment and sign shorter contracts, then expand them dramatically. Retail investors were lukewarm, and the stock traded slightly down the day after the report.

The pattern reaches beyond Palantir: enterprises try AI software quickly and cancel more readily, so a large quarter does not guarantee durable revenue. Conversion from short trials to longer contracts is the signal to watch.

item.title: Roli, maker of the Seaboard keyboard, went into administration and left customers with unfulfilled orders
item.description:
Joint administrators were appointed on October 20, the company's second insolvency, and buyers report no word on refunds or orders.

Roli, the company behind the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed. Its founder and CEO, Roland Lamb, was reportedly ousted earlier this year. On Monday the company emailed users that two licensed insolvency practitioners were appointed joint administrators on October 20. The company had already gone bankrupt once before, so this is its second insolvency.

Customers paid from hundreds to thousands of dollars and have had no response on orders or refunds. The hardware still works, but Roli instruments rely on proprietary launchers and companion apps to map sounds and configure settings. Owners worry that software support will lapse and leave the gear unusable. Roli's backers, TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, did not respond to Wired. The company was once hailed after Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony's Innovation Fund in 2018. An August registration of a new company, Instrumental Intelligence, under Lamb's name could be a route to buying Roli's assets.

item.title: EU advocate general says Google's Gemini may breach copyright by reproducing articles and getting past paywalls
item.description:
The opinion is not a ruling, but it lays out the publishers' case against Google's AI answers at the EU's top court.

An advocate general at the EU's top court has said Gemini could infringe publishers' copyright by reproducing large chunks of articles, or by getting around paywalls and similar protections to build answers. The case, brought by Hungarian website operator Like Company, is before the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. The details here come from the headline and standfirst, because the full article could not be read.

A ruling against Google could force it to pay fees for using that content, and the report says it could give online media such as Like Company a lifeline.
